title: Six New Ways Matter and Antimatter Disagree
hook: LHCb re-analysed a single B-meson decay and found six separate signatures of matter–antimatter asymmetry — including the first ever seen in a spin-3 resonance.
key_points: CP violation means a particle and its antiparticle decay at different rates — one of the conditions for a matter-dominated universe.
LHCb studied B+ → K+ π+ π−, a three-body decay whose intermediate resonances interfere, exposing many asymmetries at once.
Six CP-violating effects reached significance for the first time, including quasi-two-body violation in B+ → ρ(770)0 K+.
First evidence appeared for CP violation involving a spin-3 resonance and in elastic ππ rescattering.
Asymmetries also showed up in the interference between S- and P-wave (and S- and D-wave) contributions — effects that must come from long-distance strong dynamics.
A companion analysis relaxed old unitarity assumptions about the K*0(1430) resonance, resolving long-standing puzzles and revealing ten new intermediate decays.
content_html: The Standard Model allows matter and antimatter to behave slightly differently — a property called CP violation — and that tiny asymmetry is one of the ingredients any explanation of a matter-filled universe needs. LHCb has now squeezed six distinct CP-violating signatures out of a single decay channel, B+ → K+ π+ π−, using proton collision data recorded at the LHC in 2011–2012.
extra_html:
The trick is that a three-body decay does not happen all at once. The B meson passes through intermediate resonances — ρ(770)0, f2(1270), the broad S-wave states — whose quantum amplitudes overlap and interfere. An amplitude analysis pulls those contributions apart, and asymmetries can then appear both within a component and in the interference between components. LHCb reports discovery of quasi-two-body CP violation in B+ → ρ(770)0 K+, amplitude-level violation in B+ → f2(1270) K+, first evidence in the elastic ππ rescattering region and for any decay involving a spin-3 resonance, plus observation in S–P wave interference and evidence in S–D interference. Those last two, the collaboration notes, must be driven by long-distance strong interactions.

Two companion papers accompany the result: one reporting the branching fractions and CP asymmetries themselves using three complementary modelling approaches, and one resolving old puzzles in the B → Kππ sector — relaxing unitarity-based assumptions about the K*0(1430) resonance improved the fit enough to eliminate the ad-hoc "fX(1300)" component earlier analyses needed, and turned up ten new intermediate decays along the way. See the LHCb preprints on arXiv for the full analysis.

related.title: Antimatter
related.hook: Every particle has a mirror twin with opposite charge, and when the two meet they vanish in a flash of pure energy — yet the universe is almost entirely matter, and nobody fully knows why.

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

related.title: Measuring the force that traps a quark inside the proton
related.hook: Nobody has ever seen a free quark. A sharpened reconstruction of the actual force tugging on one inside the proton comes out looking like a string pulled at constant tension.

flashcards.prompt: What does CP violation mean, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back_html: A particle and its mirror-image antiparticle behave differently — decaying at different rates. It is one of the conditions needed for the early universe to end up with more matter than antimatter instead of annihilating to nothing.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a three-body decay like B+ → K+ π+ π− so useful for hunting CP violation?

choices.text: Its intermediate resonances overlap and interfere, so many asymmetries show up in one dataset
Three-body decays are far more common than two-body ones, giving more events
Three final-state particles cancel the detector's background exactly

flashcards.explanation_html: The decay proceeds through many intermediate resonances whose amplitudes overlap. An amplitude analysis untangles them, exposing asymmetries in each component and in the interference between partial waves.

flashcards.prompt: What made the interference-based asymmetries in this analysis especially interesting?
flashcards.back_html: CP violation showed up in S–P and S–D wave interference. Those effects can only be driven by long-distance strong-interaction dynamics, so they probe QCD as well as the weak sector.
